title: At the Pharmacy
goal: Describe a concern, collect a prescription, and ask a pharmacist to explain medicine instructions.

runs.text: Prescription
refers to an authorized medicine order; a
refill
is an additional supply under its conditions.
Over-the-counter / OTC
means available without a prescription. A
pharmacist
can discuss medicines and questions about their use. This chapter supplies no medicine recommendation or dosing instruction.

turns.speaker: Customer

runs.text: Could I speak with the pharmacist? I have an itchy rash on my arm.

turns.en: Could I speak with the pharmacist? I have an itchy rash on my arm.

turns.speaker: Pharmacist

runs.text: How long has it been there?

turns.en: How long has it been there?

runs.text: Since yesterday.

turns.speaker: Pharmacist

runs.text: Are you using any medicines, and have you had an allergic reaction to anything?

turns.en: Are you using any medicines, and have you had an allergic reaction to anything?

turns.speaker: Customer

runs.text: I take a regular prescription. I have the name here. I've had a reaction to aspirin before.

turns.en: I take a regular prescription. I have the name here. I've had a reaction to aspirin before.

turns.speaker: Pharmacist

runs.text: Tell me what happened, and we'll discuss what you need to do next.

turns.en: Tell me what happened, and we'll discuss what you need to do next.

blocks.caption: Explain symptoms and relevant information · Customer & Pharmacist

runs.text: These facts belong to the fictional customer. Do not borrow an allergy or medicine history for your actual care. “I don't know whether it's an allergy” expresses uncertainty. “I also have a runny nose” adds a symptom. “My eye is sore” locates pain without deciding that it is an infection.
“My back is killing me” is a conversational exaggeration about pain. If needed, give a concrete description afterward: “It hurts when I bend.”
Really
can strengthen a report: “It really hurts.” It can also show surprise in a reply, “Really?” The function depends on the turn.

study.title: Pick up and resolve a problem

turns.speaker: Customer

runs.text: I'm here to pick up a prescription for Taylor Reed.

turns.en: I'm here to pick up a prescription for Taylor Reed.

turns.speaker: Employee

runs.text: It isn't ready yet. We need to check something with the prescriber.

turns.en: It isn't ready yet. We need to check something with the prescriber.

turns.speaker: Customer

runs.text: What needs to be checked, and when should I contact you again?

turns.en: What needs to be checked, and when should I contact you again?

turns.speaker: Employee

runs.text: I'll ask the pharmacist to explain.

turns.en: I'll ask the pharmacist to explain.

turns.speaker: Customer

runs.text: Thank you. I'm nearly out of my regular medicine.

turns.en: Thank you. I'm nearly out of my regular medicine.

blocks.caption: Pick up and resolve a problem · Customer & Employee

runs.text: Prescriber

names the professional who issued the prescription. Ask “Are there any refills remaining?” “What's the price with my coverage?” or “Is there a different payment option?” These are questions, not promises of refill eligibility or insurance coverage.

turns.speaker: Customer

runs.text: I'm not sure I understand the label. Could you go over the directions with me?

turns.en: I'm not sure I understand the label. Could you go over the directions with me?

turns.speaker: Pharmacist

runs.text: Yes. Let's review this prescription and the label together.

turns.en: Yes. Let's review this prescription and the label together.

turns.speaker: Customer

runs.text: I need to understand the amount, timing, and how long to use it. What should I ask about food or other medicines?

turns.en: I need to understand the amount, timing, and how long to use it. What should I ask about food or other medicines?

turns.speaker: Pharmacist

runs.text: We'll check those details for this medicine.

turns.en: We'll check those details for this medicine.

turns.speaker: Customer

runs.text: Could I have the instructions in writing? And who should I contact if I notice a problem?

turns.en: Could I have the instructions in writing? And who should I contact if I notice a problem?

runs.text: Other questions: “What effects should I watch for?” “What does 'as needed' mean for this prescription?” “What should I do if I miss a dose?” Actual answers depend on the medicine and person; get them from the appropriate professional, not the sample dialogue.
Adhesive bandages
cover small areas of skin;
pain reliever
is a medicine category;
ointment
is a preparation applied to skin.
Contact lens solution
sunscreen
vitamins
, and
pregnancy test
name other products.
Tampons
absorb menstrual fluid;
condoms
are barrier products used during sex;
incontinence pads
absorb leakage;
diapers

are absorbent coverings, often for babies. Ask “Where can I find…?” without having to explain private details to everyone in the store. Product vocabulary is not an instruction to use a particular product.
Fictional case: Taylor has a prescription to collect; not ready; a rash since yesterday; regular medicine's name available; previous aspirin reaction. No dose or treatment has been chosen.
Ask to speak with the pharmacist and give the rash's location and timing. Partner asks about medicines and reactions. Use the case.
Partner says the prescription needs a prescriber check. Ask what happens next and explain that the current supply is low.
Ask for a label explanation. Partner offers to review it. Name two details you still need and request written directions.
Ask where to find one product from the vocabulary; choose only what is useful to you.
Solo: read each staff prompt and supply your customer turn. Later practice a different symptom without inventing a diagnosis.
Possibilities:
“Could you explain what needs checking?” “I'm not sure about the timing.” “Could we review that in writing?” Check whether the symptom, history, unresolved prescription issue, and question are clear.

Source note: Medicine-question categories follow [FDA pharmacist guidance](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/information-consumers-and-patients-drugs/stop-learn-go-tips-talking-your-pharmacist-learn-how-use-medicines-safely); the customer and dialogue are invented.
